prompt: Some people think that all museums and art galleries should be free for visitors, paid for by public money. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Museums and art galleries hold some of a nation's most valuable cultural treasures, and the question of who should pay for them is often debated. I largely agree that entry should be free and funded by taxation, although I accept that special exhibitions and foreign tourists could reasonably be charged.

The strongest argument for free entry is equal access. A family on a low income may hesitate to spend a significant sum simply to look at paintings or fossils, so entrance fees quietly turn culture into a privilege of the well-off. When admission costs nothing, schoolchildren, pensioners and people who would never have planned a visit can walk in on impulse and discover an interest that lasts a lifetime. Since these collections were often acquired with public money or donated to the nation, it seems fair that the public should be able to see them without paying again.

Free museums also bring wider benefits. They support education by giving teachers a resource they can use repeatedly at no cost to parents, and they attract visitors who then spend money in nearby cafés, shops and hotels, which partly offsets the public expense. In addition, a lively cultural sector strengthens a city's reputation and encourages creative industries to locate there.

Nevertheless, public budgets are limited, and money spent on museums is not available for hospitals or schools. For this reason, a mixed model is sensible. Permanent collections should be free, whereas temporary exhibitions that are expensive to stage could charge a fee, and international tourists might pay a modest contribution.

In conclusion, I believe permanent museum collections should be free to visit and supported by public funds, as this opens culture to everyone and benefits the wider economy. Limited charges for special events, however, are a reasonable way to share the cost.
band6: Museums are very important for culture and education. I agree that museums should be free because many people are poor and they cannot pay the ticket. If museums are free, more people will go there and learn about history. But the government must pay a lot of money.
notes: Band 7: "largely agree" is a precise answer to "to what extent", and the limit on that agreement (special exhibitions, tourists) is explained rather than tacked on; each body paragraph develops one reason with a consequence.

criteria.tr: Band 7 states how far it agrees and where the limit lies, then develops two reasons and a concession; band 6 agrees but ends by raising a cost problem it never answers.
criteria.cc: Band 7 moves from access to wider benefits to a compromise, with each paragraph opening on its main idea; band 6 lists reasons in one paragraph.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "equal access", "on impulse", "offsets the public expense", "permanent collections"; band 6 uses "very important" and "pay the ticket".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses conditionals, relative clauses and passives accurately; band 6 has a collocation slip ("pay the ticket") and mostly simple sentences.

prompt: Advertising aimed at children under the age of twelve should be completely banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Children today are exposed to a constant stream of advertisements on television, video platforms and mobile games. I strongly agree that advertising directed at children under twelve should be banned, because they cannot judge commercial messages fairly and the harms of such marketing outweigh its benefits.

The main reason is that young children do not fully understand what advertising is. It is widely accepted that younger children struggle to distinguish an advertisement from ordinary entertainment, and even when they can, they rarely recognise that its purpose is to persuade them. An adult knows that a cereal advert exaggerates; a six-year-old may simply believe that the product will make him stronger or more popular. Targeting people who cannot defend themselves against persuasion is, in my view, fundamentally unfair.

Furthermore, much of this advertising promotes products that are bad for children. Sugary snacks, fast food and drinks are heavily marketed with cartoon characters and free toys, contributing to unhealthy eating habits. Advertising also fuels so-called pester power: children repeatedly demand the latest toy or game, which creates conflict in families and puts pressure on parents with limited budgets.

Opponents argue that a ban would cut the income that funds children's television and that parents, not governments, should control what their children watch. However, quality children's programming can be financed through public broadcasting or subscriptions, and parents cannot realistically supervise every screen at every moment, particularly when adverts are embedded in games and online videos.

In conclusion, although a ban would have some financial costs for broadcasters, I believe it is justified. Young children deserve protection from persuasion they cannot understand, and removing such marketing would support healthier habits and calmer family life.
band6: Nowadays children watch a lot of advertisements on TV and internet. I agree that advertising for children should be banned. Because children cannot understand that adverts are not true and they always want to buy things. For example my nephew always asks his mother to buy new toys.
notes: Band 7: a strong position stated at the start and the end, two reasons explained through how children think and behave, and a rebuttal paragraph that answers the two most likely objections rather than ignoring them.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains why children are especially vulnerable and answers the main objections to a ban; band 6 gives a reason and a personal example but no development or counter-argument.
criteria.cc: Band 7 progresses from the main reason to a second reason to a rebuttal, using "Furthermore" and "However" purposefully; band 6 has a fragment after a full stop ("Because children cannot understand...").
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "pester power", "persuasion", "public broadcasting", "embedded in games"; band 6 uses "a lot of" and "buy things".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses varied complex sentences with accurate comparison; band 6 has a sentence fragment and simple clauses.

prompt: Some people believe that unpaid community service, such as helping in hospitals or cleaning parks, should be a compulsory part of secondary school education. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
In some countries, secondary pupils must complete a number of hours of volunteering before they graduate. I agree with this idea to a large extent, because community work teaches responsibility and practical skills that classrooms cannot provide, although the scheme should offer genuine choice and must not overload students.

The first benefit is the development of character. When teenagers read to elderly patients, coach younger children or help clear litter from a river bank, they see the direct effect of their effort on other people. This experience builds empathy and a sense of civic duty, and it can challenge the self-centred attitudes that adolescents are sometimes accused of. Pupils from comfortable backgrounds, in particular, may meet people whose lives are very different from their own.

Community service also brings practical advantages. Students learn to arrive on time, follow instructions and work with adults outside their family, which prepares them for the workplace. Many discover interests that shape their future; a pupil who helps in a hospital may decide to train as a nurse. In addition, charities and public services gain extra help, and the local area benefits from cleaner parks and better-supported residents.

Critics argue that compulsory volunteering is a contradiction and that students already face heavy academic pressure. These concerns are valid, but they can be addressed. If pupils choose from a wide range of activities and the required hours are modest, the work feels less like a punishment, and it need not take time away from essential study.

In conclusion, I believe a moderate requirement for community service in secondary schools is worthwhile. Provided that students have a choice of placements and the workload is reasonable, such a scheme benefits both young people and the communities they serve.
band6: Community service is a good idea for students. I agree because students can help other people and learn new skills. For example they can help old people in hospital. But some students are very busy with homework and exams so they do not have time to do it.
notes: Band 7: the extent of agreement and its conditions are clear from the first paragraph; the essay separates personal growth from practical skills, then answers the "contradiction" objection directly.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains how volunteering changes students and answers the objection about pressure; band 6 mentions the time problem but leaves it unresolved, which weakens its position.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives character, practical skills and objections a paragraph each; band 6 puts everything in four loosely linked sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "civic duty", "empathy", "placements", "self-centred"; band 6 uses "good idea", "help other people", "new skills".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses conditionals and relative clauses accurately ("If pupils choose..."); band 6 is accurate but simple.

prompt: Some people believe that competitive sports at school teach children valuable lessons for life, while others think that competition does more harm than good to children who are not naturally athletic. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Most schools organise team games, races and tournaments, but there is disagreement about whether this competitive element helps or hurts pupils. In this essay I will consider both views, and I will argue that competition is valuable, provided it is balanced with activities in which every child can succeed.

Supporters of school competition point to the lessons it teaches. Children who play in a league learn to train regularly, cooperate with teammates and accept both victory and defeat with dignity. These experiences prepare them for adult life, where they will face job interviews, deadlines and setbacks. Moreover, competition motivates many pupils to try harder than they otherwise would, and the excitement of a match can make physical activity enjoyable rather than a chore.

On the other hand, critics argue that constant competition discourages children who are less talented. A pupil who is always picked last for a team or finishes at the back of every race may conclude that sport is not for them, and this can lead to a lifelong avoidance of exercise. In addition, public failure in front of classmates can damage self-esteem and even lead to teasing. As a result, the activity that was meant to promote health ends up having the opposite effect.

In my view, the answer is not to remove competition but to broaden it. Schools should offer non-competitive options such as dance, hiking and swimming for fitness, and they can group children by ability so that contests are more even. Furthermore, rewarding effort and improvement, not only winning, ensures that weaker players feel their progress is noticed.

In conclusion, competitive sport can build discipline and resilience, yet it may alienate pupils who lack natural ability. I believe schools should keep it, but within a wider programme that allows every child to enjoy being active.
band6: Sport is very popular in schools. Some people think competition is good because children learn teamwork and how to win. Other people think it is bad for children who are not good at sport because they feel sad. I think competition is good but teachers must be careful.
notes: Band 7: both views are developed with consequences (lessons for adult life; lifelong avoidance of exercise) before the opinion, which is specific: keep competition but widen the programme in named ways.

criteria.tr: Band 7 develops both views with explained effects and gives a specific opinion; band 6 summarises each view in a sentence and ends with a vague "teachers must be careful".
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each view its own paragraph, then a paragraph for the writer's solution; band 6 lists views and opinion in one block.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "self-esteem", "resilience", "alienate", "group children by ability"; band 6 uses "good", "bad", "feel sad".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses and conditionals accurately; band 6 relies on "Some people think... Other people think".

prompt: Some people say that spending money on space exploration is a waste when there are so many problems on Earth, while others believe that it brings important benefits. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Every rocket launch costs vast sums, and critics ask why this money is not used to fight poverty or disease instead. Others insist that space research repays its cost many times over. Having considered both positions, I believe that space exploration is a worthwhile investment, although its budget should be kept in proportion to urgent needs at home.

Those who regard space programmes as wasteful make a powerful moral argument. Millions of people lack clean water, adequate healthcare or basic education, and a government that funds trips to Mars while its hospitals are underfunded appears to have the wrong priorities. In addition, the benefits of space missions can seem remote to ordinary citizens, as discovering ice on a distant moon does little to pay their rent.

However, this view underestimates how much everyday life depends on space technology. Satellites provide the weather forecasts that warn farmers and coastal towns of storms, the navigation systems in every smartphone, and much of the data scientists use to monitor deforestation, melting ice and crop failures. Research for space missions has also produced spin-off inventions in medical imaging, water purification and lightweight materials. Moreover, ambitious projects inspire young people to study science and engineering, building the skills a modern economy needs.

In my opinion, the choice is not as stark as critics suggest. Space budgets are a small part of public spending in most countries, so cancelling them would not solve global poverty. Nevertheless, governments should focus on missions with clear practical returns, such as Earth observation, and share the costs through international cooperation.

In conclusion, although the needs on our own planet are pressing, I believe space exploration should continue, since it delivers practical benefits and scientific progress that help solve some of those very problems.
band6: Space exploration is very expensive. Some people think it is a waste of money because many people are poor and hungry. Other people think it is useful because we can learn new things about the universe. In my opinion space exploration is useful because it makes new technology like satellites.
notes: Band 7: the critics' moral argument is given full weight before the essay shows concrete everyday benefits; the opinion paragraph adds a fresh point (the budget is small, focus on practical missions) instead of repeating earlier ones.

criteria.tr: Band 7 discusses both views in depth and explains concrete benefits (forecasts, navigation, monitoring); band 6 names one benefit ("new technology like satellites") without explaining it.
criteria.cc: Band 7 moves from critics to supporters to a reasoned opinion, linked by "However" and "Nevertheless"; band 6 places views and opinion in three sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "spin-off inventions", "Earth observation", "priorities", "in proportion"; band 6 repeats "space exploration" and "useful".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses complex sentences and comparatives accurately ("not as stark as"); band 6 is accurate but mostly simple.

prompt: Some people think that children are better off growing up in the countryside, while others believe that a city upbringing offers more advantages. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Parents who can choose where to raise their children often wonder whether a rural or an urban environment is better for them. Both settings offer distinct benefits, but in my view a city upbringing gives children more opportunities, provided they also have regular contact with nature.

Supporters of a rural childhood emphasise freedom and health. Children in the countryside can play outside with little traffic, explore fields and woods, and learn where food comes from by watching crops grow and animals being raised. Cleaner air and more physical activity help them stay fit, and smaller communities, in which neighbours know one another, can make young people feel safe and supported. Many adults remember such childhoods as calm and unhurried.

City advocates, by contrast, point to the range of opportunities available. Urban children usually have access to a wider choice of schools, libraries, museums, sports clubs and music lessons, which allows them to discover and develop particular talents. They also grow up among people of different backgrounds, languages and beliefs, which prepares them for a diverse adult world. In addition, better public transport lets older children travel independently, and specialist healthcare is closer at hand when it is needed.

On balance, I find the city's advantages more decisive, because educational and cultural opportunities shape a child's future in ways that are hard to replace. Rural families often have to drive long distances for activities that city children can reach by bus. The main weakness of urban life, the lack of green space, can be partly remedied by parks, weekend trips and holidays in the countryside.

In conclusion, a rural upbringing offers freedom and fresh air, whereas a city upbringing offers education and diversity. I believe the city is the better choice overall, as long as parents make sure their children still spend time in nature.
band6: Some people think the countryside is better for children because it is quiet and the air is clean. Other people think the city is better because there are good schools and many activities. I think the city is better because children can have more chances for their future.
notes: Band 7: each view is developed with specific benefits rather than single adjectives, and the opinion paragraph explains why one set of advantages is more decisive and how the city's weakness can be reduced.

criteria.tr: Band 7 discusses both views fully and explains why the city's advantages are more decisive; band 6 states a preference ("more chances for their future") without developing it.
criteria.cc: Band 7 uses one paragraph per view and a separate weighing paragraph; band 6 gives each view one sentence.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "unhurried", "diverse", "specialist healthcare", "remedied"; band 6 uses "quiet", "good schools", "many activities".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses, passives and comparatives accurately; band 6 uses only simple and compound sentences.

prompt: Some people believe that governments should tax sugary drinks and unhealthy foods to improve public health, while others argue that people should be free to decide what they eat. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Rising rates of obesity and diabetes have led several governments to introduce taxes on sugary drinks and similar products. Critics see these taxes as an intrusion into private life. Having weighed both views, I believe such taxes are justified, as long as they are combined with education and support for healthier choices.

Opponents of food taxes argue from the principle of personal freedom. Adults, they say, have the right to decide what they eat and drink, and the state should not punish them for choosing a fizzy drink or a chocolate bar. They also point out that these taxes fall most heavily on poorer households, which spend a larger share of their income on food. In their view, information campaigns would respect individual choice more than financial penalties.

Supporters, on the other hand, emphasise the wider costs of unhealthy diets. Diseases linked to excess sugar place a heavy burden on public health systems, which are funded by all taxpayers, so personal choices are not entirely private. A tax raises the price of the least healthy products and encourages manufacturers to reduce the sugar in their recipes to avoid it, which benefits even consumers who never think about nutrition. In addition, the revenue can pay for sports facilities, school meals or free drinking water.

In my opinion, the second argument is stronger, particularly where children are concerned, since they are heavily targeted by marketing and cannot judge long-term health risks. The concern about poorer families is valid, but it can be addressed by using the revenue to make fresh fruit and vegetables cheaper.

In conclusion, although freedom of choice matters, I believe governments should tax sugary and unhealthy products. When the money raised is spent on promoting healthy eating, such taxes protect public health without leaving people unable to choose.
band6: Many people eat too much sugar and they become fat. Some people think the government should put tax on sugar drinks. Other people think it is their choice what they eat. I agree with tax because it will make people healthier and the government can get more money.
notes: Band 7: the freedom argument is presented at its strongest (including the effect on poorer families) before being answered; the opinion is justified by the public cost of illness and the reformulation effect, and the main objection is resolved.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains both views and answers the strongest objection; band 6 agrees with the tax but ignores the freedom argument it has just mentioned.
criteria.cc: Band 7 progresses from opponents to supporters to a weighed opinion; band 6 lists views without a link between them.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "obesity", "intrusion", "burden", "revenue", "reduce the sugar in their recipes"; band 6 uses "become fat" and "put tax on".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses and conditionals accurately; band 6 has article and collocation errors ("put tax on sugar drinks").

prompt: An increasing number of students choose to study at universities in other countries. Do the advantages of studying abroad outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Each year, more young people leave their home countries to earn a degree overseas. Studying abroad offers academic and personal benefits, but it also involves considerable cost and difficulty. In my view, for most students who can manage the expense, the advantages clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

The academic advantages are substantial. Students can attend universities with strong reputations in their chosen field, use modern laboratories and libraries, and learn from leading researchers. In addition, studying in another language, often English, brings a level of fluency that is hard to achieve at home. Employers value international graduates, as they tend to be adaptable and comfortable working with people from different cultures.

Personal growth is an equally important benefit. Living far from family forces young people to manage money, cook, deal with officials and solve problems on their own. They make friends from many countries and learn to see their own culture from the outside, which broadens their outlook in a way that no textbook can.

There are, however, real disadvantages. Tuition fees and living costs abroad can be extremely high, and families may take on heavy debts. Moreover, many students experience loneliness and culture shock, especially in the first months, and studying complex subjects in a second language can be exhausting. Their home country may also lose talented young people if they decide to stay overseas after graduating. Nevertheless, most of these problems are temporary or can be reduced. Scholarships and part-time work can ease the financial burden, and university support services help newcomers adjust. Many graduates who remain abroad still contribute to their home countries through business links and knowledge.

In conclusion, studying abroad is expensive and emotionally challenging, yet I believe its academic, professional and personal benefits outweigh these costs for students who prepare carefully.
band6: Studying abroad has many advantages. Students can learn English and get a good degree. They can also meet people from other countries. But it is very expensive and students feel lonely. I think advantages are more than disadvantages because students can get a better job in the future.
notes: Band 7: advantages are grouped (academic, personal) and each is explained; disadvantages are treated seriously, and the end of the disadvantages paragraph explains why they are manageable, which is what "outweigh" requires.

criteria.tr: Band 7 weighs the two sides and explains why most drawbacks are temporary or reducible; band 6 says the advantages "are more" without weighing them.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each group of ideas its own paragraph and finishes with a weighing paragraph; band 6 lists points with "also" and "But".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "culture shock", "broadens their outlook", "financial burden", "adaptable"; band 6 uses "good degree", "better job", "feel lonely".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses complex sentences with accurate relative clauses; band 6 uses a non-standard comparison ("advantages are more than disadvantages").

prompt: Online shopping is replacing shopping in high-street stores in many countries. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
In many countries, a growing share of purchases is now made online rather than in traditional town-centre shops. This shift has made shopping more convenient and often cheaper, but it has also hurt local communities. Overall, I would argue that the advantages for consumers outweigh the disadvantages, although governments should act to protect town centres.

The most obvious advantage is convenience. Customers can browse thousands of products at any time of day, compare prices in seconds and have goods delivered to their door. This is especially valuable for people with disabilities, parents of young children and those living in rural areas far from large shops. Online competition also tends to lower prices, and customer reviews help buyers avoid poor-quality goods. For small producers, the internet offers access to customers around the world without the expense of renting a shop.

However, the decline of physical stores has serious consequences. As shops close, high streets lose their atmosphere and become lined with empty units, which discourages visitors and harms nearby cafés and services. Many retail jobs, often held by young or part-time workers, have disappeared. In addition, the growth in home deliveries increases van traffic and packaging waste, and frequent returns add further to the environmental cost. Some people, particularly the elderly, also miss the social contact that shopping in person provided.

Despite these drawbacks, the benefits reach almost every consumer, whereas many of the problems can be reduced. Town centres can be reinvented as places for leisure, culture and services that cannot be delivered, and stricter rules on packaging can limit waste.

In conclusion, the rise of online shopping has damaged traditional high streets and created environmental problems. On balance, however, I believe its advantages for consumers and small businesses are greater, provided town centres are adapted to new uses.
band6: Online shopping is very popular now. It is convenient because people can buy things at home and it is cheaper. But many shops in the city close and people lose their jobs. I think online shopping has more advantages because people save time and money.
notes: Band 7: advantages and disadvantages are each developed for several groups (consumers, small producers, workers, communities), and the weighing sentence explains why the balance favours the advantages.

criteria.tr: Band 7 weighs who benefits and who loses and explains why the problems can be reduced; band 6 lists one advantage and one disadvantage and decides without comparing them.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives advantages, disadvantages and the weighing their own paragraphs; band 6 has no paragraphing of ideas.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "high streets", "empty units", "packaging waste", "reinvented"; band 6 uses "very popular", "buy things", "close".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses and passives accurately; band 6 uses short, simple sentences.

prompt: In some countries, it is common for young people to take a year off between finishing school and starting university, often to travel or work. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Taking a gap year between school and university has become popular in a number of countries. Some young people use the time to travel, while others work or volunteer. I believe that, when the year is planned with a clear purpose, its advantages outweigh its disadvantages.

The main benefit is maturity. After years of following a school timetable, a period of independent work or travel teaches young people to organise their own time, handle money and cope with unfamiliar situations. As a result, many arrive at university more motivated and more certain about their choice of subject. A student who has spent several months working in a hospital, for instance, is likely to approach a medical degree with greater commitment than one who has never seen the profession in practice.

A gap year can also strengthen future employability. Paid work gives young people experience and references, and volunteering abroad develops language skills and cultural awareness that employers value. In addition, earning money before university can reduce the debts many students accumulate.

On the other hand, there are genuine risks. Without a plan, a year off can become a year of drifting, and some students lose the habit of study or decide not to return to education at all. International travel can be costly, so gap years may be available mainly to wealthier families, widening inequality. Furthermore, graduating a year later means starting a career, and earning a full salary, later than one's peers. Although these risks are real, they can be managed. A structured programme of work or volunteering, and a confirmed university place before the year begins, keep students on track.

In conclusion, a gap year carries some financial and academic risks. Nevertheless, I believe its benefits for maturity, motivation and employability outweigh them, provided that the year is used purposefully.
band6: Many students take a gap year after school. The advantage is they can travel and see the world and they can work and get money. The disadvantage is they can forget their study and it is expensive. In my opinion gap year is good if students use it well.
notes: Band 7: each advantage is explained through a consequence and an example, the disadvantages include a less obvious point (inequality), and the condition in the position ("planned with a clear purpose") is tied to how the risks are managed.

criteria.tr: Band 7 gives a clear, conditional answer and shows why the risks can be managed; band 6 has a similar condition ("if students use it well") but never explains it.
criteria.cc: Band 7 organises benefits into maturity and employability, then risks, then management; band 6 uses the formula "The advantage is... The disadvantage is...".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "drifting", "employability", "cultural awareness", "accumulate"; band 6 uses "see the world" and "get money".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses gerund subjects and comparatives accurately; band 6 omits an article ("gap year is good").

prompt: In many countries, cash is being replaced by card and mobile payments. Do the advantages of a cashless society outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Notes and coins are disappearing from daily life in many countries as people pay with cards and phones instead. A cashless economy is faster and safer in several ways, but it also excludes some groups and creates new risks. In my opinion, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that cash remains available for those who need it.

For consumers and businesses, digital payments are highly convenient. A purchase takes a second, there is no need to find an ATM or carry change, and every transaction is recorded automatically, which makes budgeting easier. Shops save the time and cost of counting, storing and transporting money, and they face a lower risk of robbery. Governments benefit as well: because electronic payments leave a record, it becomes harder to hide income from the tax authorities or to launder the proceeds of crime.

However, a world without cash has serious drawbacks. Elderly people, those with disabilities and people without bank accounts may struggle to pay for basic goods, and they risk being left behind. Electronic systems also depend on networks and electricity, so a technical failure or cyber-attack can make it impossible to buy food or fuel. In addition, every digital payment generates data about where and how people spend, which raises concerns about privacy and the power of banks and technology companies.

These problems are significant, but they can be addressed without abandoning digital payments. Governments can require shops to keep accepting cash for essential goods, offer free basic bank accounts and enforce strict rules on data protection and system security.

In conclusion, a cashless society brings speed, safety and greater transparency, while threatening to exclude vulnerable people and weaken privacy. On balance, I believe its benefits are greater, as long as cash continues to exist as a backup and personal data is properly protected.
band6: Nowadays many people pay by card or phone and they do not use cash. It is fast and easy and it is safe because thieves cannot steal money. But old people do not know how to use it. I think the advantages are more important because the world is modern now.
notes: Band 7: benefits are described for three groups (consumers, shops, governments), the disadvantages include non-obvious risks (system failure, privacy), and the weighing paragraph explains how the main harms can be limited.

criteria.tr: Band 7 weighs the sides and conditions its answer on keeping cash as a backup; band 6 justifies its choice with an irrelevant reason ("the world is modern now").
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives advantages, disadvantages and remedies a paragraph each; band 6 lists points in one paragraph.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "launder the proceeds of crime", "cyber-attack", "privacy", "transparency"; band 6 uses "fast and easy" and "old people".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses and conditionals accurately; band 6 uses simple sentences joined by "and".

prompt: The number of overweight children is rising in many countries. What are the causes of this problem, and what can be done to solve it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Childhood obesity has become a major public health concern, as overweight children are more likely to develop serious illnesses later in life. The problem has several causes related to diet and activity, and I believe that families, schools and governments must all play a part in reversing it.

The most direct cause is a change in diet. Processed snacks, fast food and sugary drinks are cheap, widely available and heavily advertised to young people, so many children consume far more calories than they need. Busy parents, who often work long hours, may rely on ready meals rather than cooking fresh food. At the same time, children are less active than previous generations. Instead of playing outside, many spend their free time on screens, and concerns about traffic and safety mean that fewer walk or cycle to school. Some schools have also reduced physical education to make room for academic subjects.

Solutions must therefore tackle both eating habits and exercise. Schools should provide nutritious meals, remove vending machines that sell sweets and fizzy drinks, and guarantee daily physical activity. Cooking lessons can teach pupils how to prepare simple, healthy dishes they can make at home. Governments can restrict advertising of unhealthy food to children and use taxes on sugary products to fund sports facilities. Local authorities, for their part, can build safe cycle routes and playgrounds so that being active becomes part of everyday life.

Parents remain crucial, as children copy the habits they see at home. Eating meals together, limiting screen time and taking part in active weekend pastimes as a family can make a lasting difference.

In conclusion, unhealthy diets and inactive lifestyles are the main causes of rising childhood obesity. I believe that solving the problem requires coordinated action by families, schools and governments to make healthy food and regular exercise the normal choice.
band6: Many children are fat nowadays. The reason is they eat junk food and play computer games all day. To solve this problem, parents should cook healthy food and schools should have more sport lessons. Also the government should make junk food more expensive so people buy less.
notes: Band 7: causes are grouped into diet and activity, each with an explanation of why the habit has changed; solutions are assigned to specific actors and match the causes, and the position (shared responsibility) frames the essay.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains why diets and activity levels have changed and proposes matching solutions for each actor; band 6 names causes in one sentence and lists solutions.
criteria.cc: Band 7 separates causes, institutional solutions and family solutions; band 6 joins solutions with "Also".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "processed snacks", "vending machines", "physical education", "inactive lifestyles"; band 6 uses "fat" and "junk food".

prompt: In many cities, older people who live alone suffer from loneliness. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to reduce it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Although cities are crowded, many elderly residents spend days without a meaningful conversation. Loneliness among older people harms both mental and physical health, and in my view it should be treated as a serious social problem that requires action from local authorities, communities and families.

Several changes in modern life lie behind this problem. Families are smaller and more mobile than in the past, so adult children frequently live in other cities or countries and can visit only occasionally. When a partner dies, an older person may suddenly find themselves alone in a home that once housed a busy family. Poor health and limited mobility make it difficult to go out, and the closure of local shops, post offices and community centres has removed many of the places where casual contact used to happen. Furthermore, the shift of services online can leave older people who are less confident with technology feeling cut off.

There are practical ways to reduce this isolation. First, local councils should fund community centres that offer affordable meals, classes and social activities, together with transport for those who cannot travel independently. Second, volunteer schemes can match older residents with people who visit or telephone them regularly, and intergenerational projects, such as students sharing housing with elderly homeowners, benefit both groups. Third, teaching older people to use video calls and messaging apps allows them to keep in touch with distant relatives. Finally, housing should be designed with shared gardens and common rooms, which encourage neighbours to meet naturally.

In conclusion, loneliness among the elderly in cities arises from family dispersal, bereavement, ill health and the loss of local meeting places. I believe it can be significantly reduced if councils, volunteers, families and planners work together to create opportunities for regular human contact.
band6: Many old people in cities are lonely. Their children are busy with work and they live far away. Old people cannot go out because they are sick. The government should build more clubs for old people and young people should visit their grandparents more often.
notes: Band 7: causes are explained as connected social changes (smaller families, bereavement, closures, digital services), and every measure answers one of them; the position that this is a serious, shared problem appears at both ends.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains several causes and links each measure to one of them; band 6 gives two causes and two general solutions.
criteria.cc: Band 7 orders measures with First, Second, Third, Finally and keeps causes in a separate paragraph; band 6 mixes causes and solutions.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "bereavement", "intergenerational", "limited mobility", "cut off"; band 6 repeats "old people".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses complex sentences with relative clauses and passives; band 6 uses short, simple sentences.

prompt: Large amounts of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans. What are the main causes of this problem, and what can be done to tackle it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Plastic waste now floats on the surface of every ocean and washes up on even the most remote beaches, where it harms wildlife and may enter the food chain. The problem results from how plastic is produced, used and discarded, and I believe it can only be solved by reducing plastic use as well as improving waste management.

The root cause is the enormous quantity of single-use plastic. Bottles, bags, food containers and packaging are cheap and convenient, so they are used once and thrown away within minutes. Much of this waste is never recycled. In many developing countries, rapid growth in consumption has outpaced the construction of collection and disposal systems, so rubbish is dumped in open sites or rivers, which carry it to the sea. Wealthier countries share responsibility, because they have often exported their plastic waste to nations that lack the means to process it. In addition, fishing nets lost or abandoned at sea and tiny particles released from synthetic clothing in washing machines add to the pollution.

Tackling the issue requires action at several points. Governments should ban or tax unnecessary single-use items, such as plastic straws and carrier bags, and require manufacturers to take responsibility for the packaging they produce. Deposit schemes for bottles give consumers a financial reason to return them. International aid can help poorer countries build proper waste collection and recycling systems, and exports of plastic waste to countries that cannot manage it should be restricted. Finally, research into biodegradable materials and filters for washing machines can reduce pollution at its source.

In conclusion, ocean plastic is caused by excessive single-use packaging, inadequate waste systems and lost fishing gear. I believe the most effective response combines lower consumption, better waste management worldwide and responsibility for producers.
band6: Plastic pollution in the ocean is a big problem. People use too many plastic bags and bottles and they throw them in the sea. The government should ban plastic bags and people should recycle more. Also companies should make products without plastic packaging.
notes: Band 7: causes cover production, consumption, poor waste systems and less obvious sources (fishing gear, synthetic fibres); the solutions mirror those causes and include an international dimension, which shows full task response.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains several causes, including the global waste trade, and proposes matching measures; band 6 assumes people throw plastic directly into the sea.
criteria.cc: Band 7 follows plastic from production to disposal in the same order for causes and solutions; band 6 lists three solutions with "Also".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "single-use", "deposit schemes", "biodegradable", "outpaced"; band 6 uses "big problem" and "too many".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses passives and relative clauses accurately; band 6 uses simple sentences throughout.

prompt: In many countries, a large number of young people are unable to find jobs after leaving school or university. What are the causes of youth unemployment, and what solutions can you suggest? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Many young people leave education full of hope, only to spend months or even years searching for work. High youth unemployment wastes talent and can lead to frustration and social unrest, so I believe it must be addressed through closer links between education and employers, as well as targeted government support.

One major cause is a mismatch between what young people learn and what employers need. Schools and universities often focus on academic knowledge, while companies are looking for practical, technical and communication skills. As a result, there may be a shortage of electricians or software testers at the same time as many graduates in other subjects cannot find suitable posts. A second cause is lack of experience. Employers prefer candidates who can be productive immediately, so school-leavers are trapped in a cycle in which they cannot get a job without experience and cannot gain experience without a job. Finally, economic downturns hit young workers hardest, as companies freeze recruitment before they dismiss existing staff.

Several measures could improve the situation. First, governments and businesses should expand apprenticeships and vocational courses, which combine study with paid work and lead directly to qualifications employers recognise. Second, universities should offer internships and careers advice from the first year, helping students choose courses with good prospects. Third, tax incentives can encourage firms to hire and train young employees, especially during recessions. In addition, support for young entrepreneurs, such as small loans and mentoring, can help some create their own jobs.

In conclusion, youth unemployment stems mainly from a skills mismatch, the experience trap and economic cycles. I believe that stronger cooperation between education and industry, supported by government incentives, offers the most effective way to help young people into work.
band6: Many young people cannot find a job after they graduate. The main reason is they do not have experience and the economy is bad. The government should help companies to give jobs to young people. Students should also learn practical skills at university so they can find a job easier.
notes: Band 7: three causes are explained as mechanisms (skills mismatch, the experience trap, recruitment freezes), and the solutions are specific and matched to them; the position is stated in the introduction and restated in the conclusion.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains how each cause produces unemployment and matches measures to causes; band 6 names two causes and suggests that the government "help companies" without saying how.
criteria.cc: Band 7 separates causes and solutions, each ordered and signposted; band 6 combines them in four sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "skills mismatch", "apprenticeships", "freeze recruitment", "tax incentives"; band 6 repeats "find a job".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses and complex comparison accurately; band 6 has a comparative error ("find a job easier").
